metadata.title: Big-O Growth on a Log-Log Chart
metadata.subject: Computer Science
metadata.objective: Compare n, n log n and n squared growth and see that a constant multiplier shifts a curve without changing its growth class.
metadata.learner: Can read functions and small tables; new to asymptotic notation.
expectedUnderstanding: On a log-log plot the growth class appears as the slope
Multiplying by a constant shifts a curve vertically without changing its slope
n squared eventually overtakes any fixed multiple of n

checkpoints.title: Two logarithmic axes
checkpoints.body: Each axis steps by powers of ten. On a log-log plot a straight line means a power law, so the slope is the growth class: n is flattest, n log n is a little steeper, n squared is steepest.

checkpoints.title: A constant lifts the line
checkpoints.body: The blue line that is rising is 1000 n. Multiplying n by 1000 lifts it three decades, but it stays parallel to n. A constant changes where the line sits, not how fast it grows.

checkpoints.title: Where the advantage ends
checkpoints.body: At n = 1000, 1000 n and n squared both equal 1,000,000. That is the crossing point. To the right of it, n squared is already above 1000 n, and the gap keeps widening.

checkpoints.title: What Big-O actually claims
checkpoints.body: Big-O names a growth class as n grows; it does not predict seconds on a machine. A larger constant can win for small n, but it cannot buy a slower class an asymptotic win.

narration.text: The chart compares operation counts for n, n log n and n squared as n runs from 1 to 10,000.
Now multiply n by 1000. The line lifts by three decades and keeps exactly the same slope.
Parallel lines mean the same growth class, even when one is far above the other.
At n = 1000 the two lines meet at one million operations; beyond that, n squared is larger.
So the constant can delay the crossover, but it cannot change the class. Big-O is about growth, not seconds.

fallback.text: On a log-log chart, n is a straight line of slope 1, n log n is slightly steeper, and n squared has slope 2. Multiplying n by 1000 moves the n line up by three decades without changing its slope. The 1000 n line crosses n squared at n = 1000, where both equal 1,000,000 operations; for larger n, n squared is above it. Big-O describes this growth class and makes no claim about runtime in seconds.

accessibility.alt: Log-log chart: n, n log n and n squared rise with different slopes. A 1000 n line starts on n, lifts three decades while staying parallel, meets n squared at n = 1000, and is overtaken after that.
